title: Taizé
hookLine: Brother Roger's community in France welcomes young people from every church to sing and pray

lines: A CHURCH FULL OF YOUNG PEOPLE.
ONE LINE, SUNG AGAIN AND AGAIN.
cards: Evening in a long, low church on a hill in the French countryside. No pews. Young people sit on the floor, on their knees, on little wooden stools, packed close.
Candles. Orange cloth. A single short line is sung, and sung again, and again, until it's less a song than a kind of breathing.
Then it changes language. Then, in the middle of the prayer, everything stops, and there's a long silence that nobody fills.
Some of the people here are Catholic, some Protestant, some Orthodox, and some aren't sure what they are.

teach.b: Roger Schutz was a young Swiss Protestant who came to the village of Taizé, in Burgundy, during the Second World War.
He bought a house close to the line that divided France, and sheltered refugees there, among them Jews fleeing the Nazis. When the house was in danger, he had to leave.
After the war he came back, and other men joined him.
They became a community of brothers, living together under vows and praying together through the day, in time from Protestant backgrounds and from the Catholic Church, all living one life.
Then young people started showing up, to pray, to talk, to work, and to sleep in tents and simple barracks. They kept coming, from many countries and churches.
The brothers wrote songs anyone could join: a single line, often from scripture or an old prayer, repeated until it sinks in. One uses an old Latin hymn: "Ubi caritas et amor, Deus ibi est."
Where charity and love are, God is there. The brothers don't try to start a new church or move anyone from theirs. They send people home, to their own parish, their own congregation.
The prayer is meant to carry the joy of the gospel, a joy that doesn't depend on things going well.

It sounds like the angel in Luke, in the King James Bible: "I bring you good tidings of great joy, which shall be to all people." To all people. In a village in Burgundy, the door stays open to whoever comes.

how: Churches of different traditions hold Taizé-style evening prayers with short repeated chants, candles, scripture and silence, and young people travel to Taizé for a week of prayer and community life.

games.q: you're Roger, in a house near a dividing line in wartime France. refugees knock on the door. what do you do?
o: send them away; it's too dangerous.
games.why: he sheltered refugees, among them Jews fleeing the Nazis, until the danger forced him to leave.

practice: Take one short line and repeat it slowly, sung, hummed or spoken: the old Latin, ubi caritas, where charity and love are, God is there, or the words of the thief beside Jesus on the cross, from Luke, which one Taizé chant sets to music: Lord, remember me when thou comest into thy kingdom.
Let it go round until you stop thinking about it, then let it fall away into silence.

wordCard.voice: Taizé. A village in France where Brother Roger's community of brothers from different churches welcomes young people to sing short chants and pray in silence.

orig.note: Latin: where charity is — the opening of an old hymn sung at Taizé.

carryVoice: Your line: the joy of the gospel. A joy that doesn't wait for things to go well. See you tomorrow.
